directAnswer: Pope Paul II was Pietro Barbo, a Venetian nobleman and nephew of Pope Eugene IV, who reigned from 1464 to 1471. He is remembered for building the Palazzo San Marco (today's Palazzo Venezia), for his clash with Rome's humanist scholars, and for fixing the Jubilee year at every 25 years.

sections.h2: A Venetian Nephew of Eugene IV
paras: Pietro Barbo was born in Venice in 1417 into a merchant family whose fortunes rose when his maternal uncle, Gabriele Condulmer, became Pope Eugene IV. Originally intended for a commercial career, Pietro turned to the Church instead, and his uncle made him a cardinal while he was still in his early twenties.

As cardinal he became known for his wealth, his love of ceremony, and a remarkable collection of gems, coins, and antiquities. When the cardinals met after the death of Pius II in 1464, they chose him quickly. Before the vote they had all signed an election agreement meant to limit the new pope's power, but Paul II set it aside once in office, which soured relations with part of the Sacred College.

sections.h2: The Abbreviators, Platina, and the Roman Academy
paras: Paul II's most lasting controversy began when he dissolved the college of abbreviators, officials who drafted papal documents and whose posts many humanists had purchased. One of them, the scholar Bartolomeo Platina, protested loudly and was imprisoned. In 1468 the pope also moved against the Roman Academy of Pomponio Leto, suspecting its members of paganizing tendencies and of plotting against him; several were jailed and later released.

Because Platina went on to write the influential Lives of the Popes, Paul II's reputation has long been shaped by a hostile witness. Modern historians treat Platina's portrait of an anti-intellectual pope with caution, noting that Paul II also protected scholars and that printing took root in Rome during his reign, with the first presses at nearby Subiaco and then in the city itself.

sections.h2: Palazzo San Marco and the Carnival of Rome
paras: Even before his election, Barbo had begun a grand residence beside his titular church of San Marco. As pope he expanded it into the Palazzo San Marco, one of the first great Renaissance palaces in Rome, now called the Palazzo Venezia. He lived there for much of his pontificate.

Paul II also enlivened the Roman Carnival, sponsoring races along the street then called the Via Lata, which later took the name Via del Corso from those races. Critics saw this as worldly display; admirers saw a ruler who wanted Rome to feel like a capital again.

sections.h2: Bohemia, the Turks, and the Jubilee Cycle
paras: In foreign affairs Paul II confronted King George of Podebrady of Bohemia, who supported the Hussite compacts that Rome had rejected. The pope excommunicated and deposed him in 1466. He also tried, with little success, to rally Christian princes against the Ottoman advance after the fall of Constantinople.

In 1470 he decreed that the Holy Year should be celebrated every 25 years, the rhythm the Church still follows today. Paul II died suddenly of a stroke in July 1471, before he could see the 1475 Jubilee he had scheduled.

keyFacts: Born Pietro Barbo in Venice in 1417
Nephew of Pope Eugene IV, who made him a cardinal
Built the Palazzo San Marco, now the Palazzo Venezia, in Rome
Dissolved the college of abbreviators and imprisoned the humanist Platina
Set the Jubilee cycle at every 25 years (1470)
Died of a stroke on 26 July 1471

faqs.question: Why did Pope Paul II quarrel with the Roman humanists?
faqs.answer: He abolished the college of abbreviators, posts many humanists had bought, and later suspected members of Pomponio Leto's Roman Academy of conspiracy and pagan sympathies. Platina, one of those imprisoned, later wrote a harsh account of him that historians now read with caution.

faqs.question: What building in Rome is linked to Paul II?
faqs.answer: The Palazzo Venezia, originally called the Palazzo San Marco, which he began as a cardinal and expanded as pope. It is one of the earliest major Renaissance palaces in Rome.

faqs.question: Did Paul II change how often Jubilee years are held?
faqs.answer: Yes. In 1470 he fixed the ordinary Holy Year at every 25 years, the interval still used by the Church.

directAnswer: Pope Sixtus IV was Francesco della Rovere, a Franciscan theologian from Liguria who reigned from 1471 to 1484. He built the Sistine Chapel, which bears his name, refounded the Vatican Library, and promoted devotion to the Immaculate Conception, but his pontificate was also marked by heavy nepotism and entanglement in the Pazzi conspiracy against the Medici.

sections.h2: From Franciscan Theologian to Pope
paras: Francesco della Rovere was born in 1414 at Celle Ligure, near Savona, to a family of modest means. He joined the Franciscans as a boy, studied and taught theology at several Italian universities, and earned a reputation as a gifted preacher and scholar. In 1464 he was elected Minister General of his order, and Paul II made him a cardinal in 1467.

His theological writings included works on the Immaculate Conception, then a disputed question between Franciscans and Dominicans. Elected pope in August 1471, he became the first Franciscan to hold the office in nearly two centuries and took the name Sixtus.

sections.h2: Building the Sistine Chapel and the Vatican Library
paras: Sixtus IV transformed the face of Rome. He rebuilt the old Palatine chapel of the Vatican as a new chapel, completed around 1481, whose walls were frescoed with scenes from the lives of Moses and Christ by Botticelli, Perugino, Ghirlandaio, Cosimo Rosselli and others. It has been known ever since as the Sistine Chapel, and it is where conclaves are held today.

He also gave the Vatican Library a permanent foundation in 1475, appointing the humanist Platina as librarian, a scene later painted by Melozzo da Forli. Other projects included the Ponte Sisto over the Tiber and the restoration of churches and streets. In 1471 he gave a group of ancient bronzes to the people of Rome, a gift regarded as the origin of the Capitoline Museums.

sections.h2: Nephews, the Pazzi Conspiracy, and War with Florence
paras: Sixtus IV relied heavily on relatives, raising several nephews to the cardinalate, including Pietro Riario and Giuliano della Rovere, the future Julius II, and granting lands to others, especially Girolamo Riario. This nepotism drew criticism even in an age used to family politics.

In 1478 the Pazzi family of Florence, with the involvement of Girolamo Riario and the Archbishop of Pisa, attacked Lorenzo and Giuliano de' Medici during Mass in Florence Cathedral. Giuliano was killed and Lorenzo escaped. Historians debate how much Sixtus knew; he is generally thought to have favored removing the Medici from power while not sanctioning murder. The aftermath led to excommunications, an interdict on Florence, and two years of war.

sections.h2: The Spanish Inquisition and the Immaculate Conception
paras: At the request of Ferdinand and Isabella, Sixtus IV in 1478 authorized the Spanish monarchs to appoint inquisitors to investigate converts from Judaism suspected of secretly practicing their former faith. Within a few years he complained in writing about the harshness of the Spanish tribunals, but the institution remained largely under royal control.

In doctrine, Sixtus approved a Mass and Office for the feast of the Immaculate Conception in 1476 and later forbade either side in the debate to accuse the other of heresy. He died in August 1484 and was buried in a bronze tomb by Antonio Pollaiuolo, now in the treasury museum of St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Born Francesco della Rovere at Celle Ligure in 1414
Franciscan friar and Minister General of the order (1464)
Built the Sistine Chapel, completed around 1481
Refounded the Vatican Library in 1475
Authorized the Spanish Inquisition in 1478
Uncle of the future Pope Julius II

faqs.question: Is the Sistine Chapel named after Pope Sixtus IV?
faqs.answer: Yes. Sistine comes from Sixtus. He built the chapel and commissioned its wall frescoes; the famous ceiling was painted later by Michelangelo for his nephew, Julius II.

faqs.question: Was Sixtus IV involved in the Pazzi conspiracy?
faqs.answer: His nephew Girolamo Riario was among the plotters, and the pope supported efforts to unseat the Medici. Whether he knew murder was planned is debated; most historians think he did not approve of killing.

faqs.question: What did Sixtus IV do for the Immaculate Conception?
faqs.answer: A Franciscan who had written on the subject, he approved a Mass and Office for the feast in 1476 and barred both sides of the theological debate from calling the other heretical.

directAnswer: Pope Innocent VIII was Giovanni Battista Cibo of Genoa, who reigned from 1484 to 1492. His pontificate is remembered for the bull Summis desiderantes affectibus on witchcraft, a costly war with Naples, the custody of the Ottoman prince Cem in Rome, and close ties to the Medici of Florence.

sections.h2: A Genoese Cardinal Elected in 1484
paras: Giovanni Battista Cibo was born in Genoa in 1432 to a family of Roman senatorial standing. Before his ordination he fathered children, whom he later acknowledged openly as pope, including his son Franceschetto. He entered papal service, became bishop of Savona and later Molfetta, and was created a cardinal by Sixtus IV in 1473.

In the conclave of August 1484, Cardinal Giuliano della Rovere played a decisive role in securing Cibo's election. Innocent VIII was regarded as amiable but easily guided, and della Rovere remained one of the most influential men at his court.

sections.h2: Summis Desiderantes and the Witch Trials
paras: In December 1484 Innocent VIII issued the bull Summis desiderantes affectibus at the request of the Dominican inquisitor Heinrich Kramer, granting him and a colleague authority to pursue alleged witchcraft in parts of Germany. Kramer later printed the bull at the front of his notorious handbook, the Malleus Maleficarum, lending it an air of papal approval it did not formally have.

In Spain, Innocent VIII in 1487 confirmed Tomas de Torquemada as grand inquisitor of the Spanish tribunal established under Sixtus IV. He also had a commission examine the 900 theses of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, several of which were condemned in 1487.

sections.h2: War with Naples and the Medici Alliance
paras: Early in his reign the pope was drawn into the so-called Barons' War, backing rebellious nobles against King Ferrante of Naples. The conflict drained the papal treasury and ended in 1486 without lasting gains.

Innocent VIII then drew close to Lorenzo de' Medici. His son Franceschetto married Lorenzo's daughter Maddalena, and in 1489 the pope named Lorenzo's thirteen-year-old son Giovanni a cardinal, on condition that the appointment remain secret for three years. That boy would become Pope Leo X.

sections.h2: Prince Cem and the Holy Lance
paras: From 1489 Rome held as an honored captive Prince Cem, brother and rival of the Ottoman sultan Bayezid II. In return for keeping him from leading a revolt, the sultan paid the papacy an annual sum and in 1492 sent the relic venerated as the Holy Lance, which is still kept at St. Peter's.

Innocent VIII also built the Belvedere villa on the Vatican hill. He died on 25 July 1492, months after the fall of Granada ended Muslim rule in Spain and only days before Columbus sailed. Lurid stories about his final days circulated later but are not supported by reliable sources.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Battista Cibo in Genoa in 1432
Issued the bull Summis desiderantes affectibus on witchcraft (1484)
Confirmed Tomas de Torquemada as Spanish grand inquisitor (1487)
Made Giovanni de' Medici, the future Leo X, a cardinal at 13
Received the relic of the Holy Lance from Sultan Bayezid II (1492)
Died 25 July 1492

faqs.question: Did Innocent VIII approve the Malleus Maleficarum?
faqs.answer: No. He issued Summis desiderantes affectibus in 1484 empowering inquisitors in Germany, and the author of the Malleus later printed that bull in his book. The pope never formally endorsed the handbook itself.

faqs.question: Who was Prince Cem and why was he in Rome?
faqs.answer: Cem was a brother and rival of Sultan Bayezid II. Held in papal custody from 1489, he was a political asset; the sultan paid for his detention and sent the relic of the Holy Lance to Rome.

faqs.question: How was Innocent VIII connected to the Medici?
faqs.answer: His son married Lorenzo de' Medici's daughter, and he named Lorenzo's son Giovanni a cardinal at age 13. Giovanni later became Pope Leo X.

directAnswer: Pope Alexander VI was Rodrigo de Borja (Borgia), a Valencian-born cardinal and nephew of Callixtus III, who reigned from 1492 to 1503. He issued the bull Inter caetera dividing newly explored lands between Spain and Portugal, and his openly acknowledged children, including Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia, made his pontificate one of the most controversial of the Renaissance.

sections.h2: Rodrigo Borgia, Vice-Chancellor of the Church
paras: Rodrigo de Borja was born around 1431 at Xativa in the Kingdom of Valencia, part of the Crown of Aragon. His uncle Alfonso de Borja became Pope Callixtus III in 1455 and made Rodrigo a cardinal the following year, then vice-chancellor of the Church, an office he held for some 35 years under five popes.

He was an able administrator and immensely wealthy. He also fathered several children, most notably Cesare, Juan, Lucrezia and Jofre by Vannozza dei Cattanei. In August 1492 he was elected pope; contemporaries alleged that votes had been bought, a charge many historians consider likely.

sections.h2: Inter Caetera and the New World
paras: Months after Columbus returned from his first voyage, Alexander VI issued a series of bulls in 1493, chief among them Inter caetera, that drew a line in the Atlantic and assigned lands beyond it to Castile, with the duty of evangelizing their peoples. Spain and Portugal adjusted the line themselves in the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494.

In 1496 he granted Ferdinand and Isabella the title of Catholic Monarchs. These decisions shaped the colonial map of the Americas for centuries and remain a subject of debate in discussions of conquest and missionary history.

sections.h2: The French Invasion and Savonarola
paras: In 1494 King Charles VIII of France invaded Italy to claim Naples and entered Rome, forcing the pope to negotiate from Castel Sant'Angelo. Alexander VI then helped organize the League of Venice that pushed the French out.

In Florence the Dominican preacher Girolamo Savonarola denounced corruption in the Church and the papacy. Alexander VI ordered him to stop preaching and excommunicated him in 1497. In 1498 Florentine authorities tried and executed Savonarola, an episode that remains part of the pope's contested legacy.

sections.h2: Cesare Borgia and the Papal States
paras: After the murder of his son Juan in 1497, which was never solved, Alexander VI spoke of reforming his life and the Curia, but the plans faded. Instead he backed Cesare, who renounced the cardinalate and led campaigns to subdue the lords of the Romagna, building a Borgia power base within the Papal States.

Alexander VI celebrated the Jubilee of 1500 and commissioned Pinturicchio to decorate the Borgia Apartments in the Vatican. He died on 18 August 1503, probably of malaria. Later Catholic historians, including Ludwig von Pastor, judged his private life severely while acknowledging his political skill; the Church has never defended his conduct.

keyFacts: Born Rodrigo de Borja at Xativa, Kingdom of Valencia, around 1431
Nephew of Pope Callixtus III; vice-chancellor of the Church for decades
Issued Inter caetera (1493) on lands of the New World
Father of Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia among other children
Excommunicated Girolamo Savonarola (1497)
Died 18 August 1503 in Rome

faqs.question: What was the bull Inter caetera?
faqs.answer: A 1493 decree of Alexander VI that drew a line through the Atlantic and assigned newly found lands west of it to Castile, with a charge to evangelize. Spain and Portugal moved the line in the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas.

faqs.question: Did Pope Alexander VI have children?
faqs.answer: Yes. He acknowledged several children, the best known being Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia, born to Vannozza dei Cattanei before his election.

faqs.question: How does the Church view Alexander VI today?
faqs.answer: Catholic historians have long criticized his private life and nepotism. His case is often cited to show that the authority of the papal office does not depend on the personal holiness of the man who holds it.

directAnswer: Pope Pius III was Francesco Todeschini Piccolomini, a nephew of Pope Pius II, who was elected in September 1503 and died 26 days later. Already gravely ill at his election, he is best remembered for founding the Piccolomini Library in Siena Cathedral.

sections.h2: Nephew and Heir of Pius II
paras: Francesco Todeschini was the son of Laudomia Piccolomini, sister of the humanist pope Pius II. His uncle adopted him into the Piccolomini family, made him archbishop of Siena, and created him a cardinal in 1460 while he was still in his early twenties.

Over four decades as a cardinal he gained a reputation for integrity and learning and served on diplomatic missions, including to Germany. In 1492 he commissioned the Piccolomini Library in Siena Cathedral to honor his uncle; its walls were frescoed by Pinturicchio with scenes from the life of Pius II.

sections.h2: A Twenty-Six-Day Pontificate
paras: After the death of Alexander VI in August 1503, Rome was tense, with the troops of Cesare Borgia nearby and rival factions in the Sacred College. The cardinals settled on the elderly and ailing Piccolomini as a compromise on 22 September, and he took the name Pius III in memory of his uncle.

Because he was not yet a priest, he was ordained and consecrated bishop in the days after his election and was crowned on 8 October. He hoped to call a reforming council and to restore peace, but illness overtook him and he died on 18 October 1503. Little else can be said of his short reign; the conclave that followed elected Giuliano della Rovere as Julius II.

keyFacts: Born Francesco Todeschini; took the Piccolomini name from his uncle Pius II
Cardinal from 1460 and archbishop of Siena
Commissioned the Piccolomini Library in Siena Cathedral (1492)
Elected 22 September 1503 as a compromise candidate
Died 18 October 1503 after a 26-day reign

faqs.question: Why was Pius III's reign so short?
faqs.answer: He was already elderly and seriously ill when elected, and he died less than four weeks later, on 18 October 1503.

faqs.question: What is the Piccolomini Library?
faqs.answer: A richly frescoed hall in Siena Cathedral that Cardinal Piccolomini, the future Pius III, commissioned in 1492 to honor his uncle Pius II. Pinturicchio painted its scenes of Pius II's life.

directAnswer: Pope Julius II was Giuliano della Rovere, nephew of Sixtus IV, who reigned from 1503 to 1513. Known as the warrior pope, he personally led campaigns to restore the Papal States, laid the foundation stone of the new St. Peter's Basilica, founded the Swiss Guard, commissioned Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling and Raphael's Vatican rooms, and convened the Fifth Lateran Council.

sections.h2: Cardinal della Rovere and His Rivalry with the Borgias
paras: Giuliano della Rovere was born in 1443 at Albisola near Savona. When his uncle became Sixtus IV in 1471, Giuliano was made a cardinal and soon became one of the most powerful men in the Curia, helping to elect Innocent VIII.

He bitterly opposed Alexander VI and spent much of that pontificate in exile in France. After Pius III's brief reign, he won the conclave of 1 November 1503 in a matter of hours, reportedly having secured support through generous promises.

sections.h2: The Warrior Pope and the Italian Wars
paras: Julius II set out to recover papal territory lost or held by local lords and foreign powers. In 1506 he rode at the head of his troops to take Perugia and Bologna. He joined the League of Cambrai against Venice in 1508, then turned against France with the Holy League of 1511, determined to drive the French from Italy.

In January 1506 a contingent of Swiss soldiers arrived in Rome to serve as his guard, the origin of the Pontifical Swiss Guard that still protects the pope. Machiavelli discussed Julius in The Prince as a bold ruler whose impetuous style happened to suit his times.

sections.h2: Bramante, Michelangelo, and Raphael
paras: On 18 April 1506 Julius laid the foundation stone of a new St. Peter's Basilica designed by Bramante, replacing the old Constantinian church. To fund the vast project he authorized indulgence preaching, a practice that would become a flashpoint under his successor.

He summoned Michelangelo, first to design his tomb and then to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling, completed in 1512. Raphael began the frescoes of the papal apartments now called the Raphael Rooms, including the School of Athens. Julius also displayed ancient sculptures such as the Laocoon, found in 1506, in the Belvedere courtyard, the seed of the Vatican Museums.

sections.h2: The Fifth Lateran Council and the Church in the Americas
paras: When French-backed cardinals summoned a rival council at Pisa in 1511 to challenge him, Julius responded by convening the Fifth Lateran Council, which opened in Rome in May 1512. He also issued a bull declaring simoniacal papal elections invalid.

In the New World he established the first dioceses in the Americas in 1511, on Hispaniola and Puerto Rico, and granted the Spanish crown broad rights of patronage over the Church there. Julius II died on 21 February 1513, leaving the papacy politically stronger and Rome transformed artistically.

keyFacts: Born Giuliano della Rovere at Albisola in 1443; nephew of Sixtus IV
Founded the Pontifical Swiss Guard (1506)
Laid the foundation stone of the new St. Peter's Basilica (18 April 1506)
Commissioned Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508 to 1512)
Convened the Fifth Lateran Council (1512)
Erected the first dioceses in the Americas (1511)

faqs.question: Why is Julius II called the warrior pope?
faqs.answer: He personally led papal armies, most famously in 1506 against Perugia and Bologna, and formed military alliances to recover the Papal States and expel the French from Italy.

faqs.question: Did Julius II found the Swiss Guard?
faqs.answer: Yes. The first Swiss guardsmen arrived in Rome in January 1506 at his request, and the corps has served the popes ever since.

faqs.question: What did Julius II commission from Michelangelo?
faqs.answer: His tomb, which includes the famous Moses now in San Pietro in Vincoli, and the Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted between 1508 and 1512.

directAnswer: Pope Leo X was Giovanni de' Medici, son of Lorenzo the Magnificent, who reigned from 1513 to 1521. A lavish patron of Raphael and Renaissance learning, he closed the Fifth Lateran Council, concluded the Concordat of Bologna with France, and excommunicated Martin Luther in 1521 after the indulgence controversy that launched the Protestant Reformation.

sections.h2: A Medici Cardinal at Thirteen
paras: Giovanni de' Medici was born in Florence on 11 December 1475, the second son of Lorenzo the Magnificent. He received a humanist education and was named a cardinal by Innocent VIII in 1489 at the age of thirteen, taking his place in the Sacred College in 1492.

When the Medici were expelled from Florence in 1494 he lived in exile and traveled, returning to restore his family's rule in 1512. Elected pope in March 1513 at 37, he was still only a deacon and was ordained priest and consecrated bishop after the conclave.

sections.h2: Closing the Lateran Council and the Concordat of Bologna
paras: Leo X continued the Fifth Lateran Council begun by Julius II and brought it to a close in March 1517. Its reform decrees were modest and largely unenforced, a missed opportunity on the eve of the Reformation.

In 1516 he concluded the Concordat of Bologna with King Francis I, giving the French crown the right to nominate bishops and abbots in France while restoring papal confirmation. The agreement governed Church and state in France until the Revolution. In 1517 a plot by several cardinals to poison him was uncovered; Cardinal Alfonso Petrucci was executed, and Leo then created 31 new cardinals in a single consistory.

sections.h2: Indulgences, Luther, and Exsurge Domine
paras: To fund the rebuilding of St. Peter's, Leo X renewed the indulgence campaign, including an arrangement in Germany with Archbishop Albert of Brandenburg. The preaching of Johann Tetzel prompted Martin Luther to post his 95 Theses in October 1517.

Rome at first treated the matter as a friars' quarrel. In June 1520 Leo issued the bull Exsurge Domine condemning 41 propositions from Luther's writings, and in January 1521 the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem excommunicated him. That same year Leo granted Henry VIII the title Defender of the Faith for his treatise defending the seven sacraments.

sections.h2: Raphael, Rome, and an Empty Treasury
paras: Leo X made Rome the cultural capital of Europe. Raphael continued the Vatican rooms, designed the tapestries for the Sistine Chapel, and became architect of St. Peter's. The pope reorganized the Roman university, the Sapienza, and supported scholars of Greek and classical antiquity. A white elephant named Hanno, a gift from the King of Portugal, became a celebrity of his court.

His generosity, wars such as the campaign to seize Urbino, and costly festivities left the papacy deep in debt. Leo X died unexpectedly on 1 December 1521, at a moment when the religious crisis in Germany was only beginning.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni de' Medici in Florence on 11 December 1475
Son of Lorenzo the Magnificent; cardinal at age 13
Closed the Fifth Lateran Council (1517)
Signed the Concordat of Bologna with Francis I of France (1516)
Issued Exsurge Domine (1520) and excommunicated Martin Luther (1521)
Named Henry VIII Defender of the Faith (1521)

faqs.question: Was Leo X the pope who excommunicated Martin Luther?
faqs.answer: Yes. He condemned Luther's teachings in the bull Exsurge Domine in 1520 and excommunicated him with Decet Romanum Pontificem in January 1521.

faqs.question: Was Leo X a priest when he was elected pope?
faqs.answer: No. He was a cardinal deacon at his election in 1513 and was ordained a priest and consecrated a bishop shortly afterward.

faqs.question: Why did Leo X give Henry VIII the title Defender of the Faith?
faqs.answer: In 1521 Henry wrote a treatise defending the seven sacraments against Luther, and Leo rewarded him with the title, which English monarchs still use.

directAnswer: Pope Adrian VI was Adriaan Florensz of Utrecht, a Louvain theologian and former tutor of Emperor Charles V, who reigned from 1522 to 1523. The only Dutch pope and the last non-Italian until John Paul II in 1978, he tried to reform the Roman Curia and publicly acknowledged its share of blame for the crisis of the Reformation.

sections.h2: Scholar of Louvain and Tutor of Charles V
paras: Adriaan Florensz was born in Utrecht on 2 March 1459 to a family of modest means. He studied at the University of Louvain, where he became a professor of theology and later its vice-chancellor, known for austere habits and serious scholarship.

In 1507 he was chosen as tutor to the young Charles of Habsburg, the future Emperor Charles V. He went on to serve in Spain as bishop of Tortosa, inquisitor general, and regent during Charles's absences. Leo X made him a cardinal in 1517.

sections.h2: An Unexpected Election in Absentia
paras: After the death of Leo X, a deadlocked conclave elected Adrian on 9 January 1522, though he was in Spain and had not attended. He kept his own baptismal name, becoming Adrian VI, and did not reach Rome until late August 1522.

Romans accustomed to Medici splendor found the frugal northerner baffling. He cut expenses, reduced the papal household, and showed little interest in the arts, which made him deeply unpopular with the city's courtiers and artists.

sections.h2: The Confession Read at Nuremberg
paras: Adrian VI firmly rejected Luther's theology and called on the German princes to enforce the condemnation issued at Worms. Yet in instructions sent with his legate Francesco Chieregati to the Diet of Nuremberg in 1522 and 1523, he made a striking admission: the evils afflicting the Church had spread from the head downward, beginning with the Roman Curia, and he promised reform.

The candor won him admirers among later reformers, but the German estates were not satisfied, and his attempts to curb abuses in the Curia met stubborn resistance. He also tried without success to unite Christian princes against the Ottomans, who captured the island of Rhodes from the Knights of St. John in December 1522.

sections.h2: Death and Burial in Santa Maria dell'Anima
paras: In 1523 Adrian VI canonized Antoninus of Florence and Benno of Meissen. Worn down by opposition and illness, he died on 14 September 1523 after barely a year in Rome.

He was eventually buried in Santa Maria dell'Anima, the church of the German-speaking community in Rome, where his tomb laments that even the best of men depend on the times in which they live. No non-Italian would be elected pope again for 455 years.

keyFacts: Born Adriaan Florensz in Utrecht on 2 March 1459
Professor and vice-chancellor at the University of Louvain
Tutor of the future Emperor Charles V and regent of Spain
Elected in absentia on 9 January 1522
Only Dutch pope; last non-Italian pope until 1978
Buried in Santa Maria dell'Anima, Rome

faqs.question: What did Adrian VI admit at the Diet of Nuremberg?
faqs.answer: Through his legate Chieregati, he acknowledged that abuses in the Church had begun at its head, in the Roman Curia, and pledged reform, while still insisting that Luther's teaching be condemned.

faqs.question: Was Adrian VI the last non-Italian pope before John Paul II?
faqs.answer: Yes. After his death in 1523, every pope was Italian until the election of the Polish John Paul II in 1978.

faqs.question: Why was Adrian VI unpopular in Rome?
faqs.answer: He was a frugal foreigner who cut spending, reduced the court, and showed little enthusiasm for the lavish artistic patronage Romans expected after Leo X.

directAnswer: Pope Clement VII was Giulio de' Medici, cousin of Leo X, who reigned from 1523 to 1534. His pontificate saw the Sack of Rome by imperial troops in 1527, his refusal to annul the marriage of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, the coronation of Charles V at Bologna, and the approval of the Capuchin friars.

sections.h2: Giulio de' Medici, Cousin of Leo X
paras: Giulio de' Medici was born in Florence in 1478, the son of Giuliano de' Medici, who was killed in the Pazzi conspiracy a month before his birth. He was raised in the household of his uncle Lorenzo the Magnificent alongside his cousin Giovanni.

When Giovanni became Leo X, he made Giulio archbishop of Florence and a cardinal in 1513, and Giulio became his chief adviser. After the short reign of Adrian VI, Giulio was elected on 19 November 1523 and took the name Clement VII.

sections.h2: Between Emperor and King: The Sack of Rome
paras: Clement VII inherited a papacy caught in the rivalry between Emperor Charles V and King Francis I of France. His shifting alliances, culminating in the League of Cognac with France in 1526, angered the emperor.

In May 1527 unpaid imperial troops, many of them German mercenaries, stormed Rome and sacked it for weeks. Most of the Swiss Guard died on 6 May defending the pope's escape to Castel Sant'Angelo, a sacrifice still commemorated each year when new guards are sworn in. Clement was held for months before escaping to Orvieto. He later reconciled with Charles and crowned him emperor at Bologna in February 1530, the last papal coronation of an emperor.

sections.h2: The King's Great Matter
paras: Henry VIII sought an annulment of his marriage to Catherine of Aragon, the aunt of Charles V. Clement delayed for years, sending Cardinal Campeggio to hear the case in England in 1529 before recalling it to Rome.

After Henry married Anne Boleyn in 1533, Clement declared the action invalid and threatened excommunication, and in March 1534 he ruled that Henry's marriage to Catherine was valid. Within months Parliament passed the Act of Supremacy, separating the Church of England from Rome.

sections.h2: Capuchins, Theatines, and the Last Judgment
paras: Clement VII approved the Theatines in 1524 and the Capuchin reform of the Franciscans in 1528, both important in the Catholic renewal that followed. In 1533 he arranged the marriage of his young relative Catherine de' Medici to the future Henry II of France.

A patron of Michelangelo, he oversaw work on the Medici Chapel in Florence and asked the artist to paint the Last Judgment on the Sistine altar wall, a work carried out under his successor. That same year he heard an explanation of Copernicus's ideas about the sun-centered universe in the Vatican gardens. Clement VII died on 25 September 1534.

keyFacts: Born Giulio de' Medici in Florence in 1478; cousin of Leo X
Sack of Rome by imperial troops in May 1527
Crowned Charles V emperor at Bologna in 1530
Refused Henry VIII's annulment; upheld his marriage to Catherine in 1534
Approved the Theatines (1524) and Capuchins (1528)
Died 25 September 1534

faqs.question: What happened to Clement VII during the Sack of Rome?
faqs.answer: As imperial troops entered Rome on 6 May 1527, he fled to Castel Sant'Angelo while the Swiss Guard fought a rearguard action. He remained a virtual prisoner for months before escaping to Orvieto.

faqs.question: Why did Clement VII refuse Henry VIII's annulment?
faqs.answer: He was not persuaded the marriage to Catherine of Aragon was invalid, and political pressure from her nephew Charles V weighed heavily. In 1534 he formally declared the marriage valid.

faqs.question: Did Clement VII commission the Last Judgment?
faqs.answer: He asked Michelangelo to paint it on the Sistine altar wall shortly before his death; the work was carried out under Paul III and finished in 1541.

directAnswer: Pope Paul III was Alessandro Farnese, who reigned from 1534 to 1549. He opened the Council of Trent in 1545, approved the Society of Jesus in 1540, established the Roman Inquisition, and named Michelangelo chief architect of St. Peter's, setting the Catholic Reformation in motion.

sections.h2: Alessandro Farnese, a Renaissance Cardinal
paras: Alessandro Farnese was born in 1468 into a noble family of the Papal States and received a humanist education, partly in the circle of Lorenzo de' Medici in Florence. Alexander VI made him a cardinal in 1493; the advancement was widely linked to his sister Giulia's closeness to that pope.

Before his priestly ordination he fathered several children, including Pier Luigi Farnese. He later reformed his life and became a respected senior cardinal. Elected unanimously in October 1534, he was then the dean of the Sacred College.

sections.h2: Reform Commission, Jesuits, and the Roman Inquisition
paras: Paul III raised reform-minded men to the cardinalate, including Gasparo Contarini, Reginald Pole, Gian Pietro Carafa and John Fisher, who was executed by Henry VIII weeks after his appointment in 1535. In 1537 a commission of these reformers delivered a frank report on abuses in the Church, the Consilium de emendanda ecclesia.

On 27 September 1540 the bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae approved the Society of Jesus founded by Ignatius of Loyola. In 1542 Paul III established the Congregation of the Roman Inquisition to oppose Protestant teaching in Italy, and in 1544 he approved the Ursulines. In 1537 he had also issued Sublimis Deus, affirming that the native peoples of the Americas were rational human beings who must not be deprived of liberty or property.

sections.h2: Opening the Council of Trent
paras: After years of negotiation with Charles V and Francis I, the Council of Trent opened on 13 December 1545. In its first sessions it defined the canon of Scripture, affirmed the role of Tradition, and issued a major decree on justification.

In 1547 Paul III moved the council to Bologna, partly over plague and partly over tension with the emperor, and its work stalled. Meanwhile he carried out the final sentence of excommunication against Henry VIII in 1538, following the dissolution of England's monasteries.

sections.h2: Michelangelo, St. Peter's, and the Farnese Family
paras: Paul III had Michelangelo complete the Last Judgment in 1541, and in 1546 appointed him chief architect of St. Peter's, where he designed the great dome. Michelangelo also redesigned the Capitoline Hill and worked on the Palazzo Farnese. Titian painted the pope's famous portraits.

Paul III did not escape nepotism. He made two teenage grandsons cardinals and in 1545 created the duchy of Parma and Piacenza for his son Pier Luigi, who was assassinated two years later. The pope died on 10 November 1549, having launched the reform that would define the Church for centuries.

keyFacts: Born Alessandro Farnese in 1468; cardinal from 1493
Approved the Society of Jesus on 27 September 1540
Established the Roman Inquisition (1542)
Issued Sublimis Deus on the rights of Indigenous peoples (1537)
Opened the Council of Trent on 13 December 1545
Appointed Michelangelo chief architect of St. Peter's (1546)

faqs.question: Did Paul III approve the Jesuits?
faqs.answer: Yes. On 27 September 1540 his bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae formally approved the Society of Jesus founded by St. Ignatius of Loyola and his companions.

faqs.question: What was the Consilium de emendanda ecclesia?
faqs.answer: A 1537 report by a commission of cardinals and prelates appointed by Paul III that candidly listed abuses in the Church, especially in the Curia, and proposed remedies.

faqs.question: What was Sublimis Deus?
faqs.answer: A 1537 bull of Paul III declaring that the Indigenous peoples of the Americas were true human beings capable of receiving the faith who must not be enslaved or robbed of their property.

directAnswer: Pope Julius III was Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte, a Roman-born canon lawyer who had presided over the opening of the Council of Trent, and he reigned from 1550 to 1555. He reconvened the council in 1551, founded the Collegium Germanicum with St. Ignatius of Loyola, and saw England briefly reconciled with Rome under Mary I, though his favoritism toward an adopted nephew caused lasting scandal.

sections.h2: Papal Legate at the Opening of Trent
paras: Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte was born in Rome in 1487 to a family from Monte San Savino in Tuscany. Trained in law, he rose through the Curia, served as archbishop of Siponto, and was made a cardinal by Paul III in 1536.

In 1545 he was one of the three papal legates who presided over the first sessions of the Council of Trent, alongside Marcello Cervini and Reginald Pole. After a conclave of more than ten weeks, he was elected pope on 7 February 1550 and took the name Julius in honor of Julius II, who had first advanced his family.

sections.h2: Reconvening the Council in 1551
paras: Julius III reopened the Council of Trent at Trent in May 1551. In this second period the council issued important decrees on the Eucharist, penance and anointing of the sick, and some Protestant envoys from Germany briefly attended.
In April 1552 the revolt of Maurice of Saxony against Charles V threatened the city, and the council was suspended. It would not meet again for nearly ten years.

sections.h2: The Jesuits, the Collegium Germanicum, and England
paras: Julius III confirmed and expanded the Society of Jesus in 1550 with the bull Exposcit debitum. In 1552, at Ignatius of Loyola's urging, he founded the Collegium Germanicum in Rome to train priests for the German-speaking lands where Protestantism had spread.

When Mary I became queen of England in 1553, Julius sent Cardinal Pole as legate, and in November 1554 Parliament restored communion with Rome. The reconciliation lasted only until Mary's death in 1558.

sections.h2: Villa Giulia, Palestrina, and the Innocenzo Scandal
paras: Julius III spent heavily on the Villa Giulia outside Rome's walls, a refined suburban retreat designed with the help of Vignola and Ammannati that now houses the national Etruscan museum. He brought the composer Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina to Rome as choirmaster of the Cappella Giulia in 1551 and later admitted him to the papal choir.

Shortly after his election, Julius made Innocenzo Ciocchi del Monte, a teenage youth of humble origins whom his brother had adopted, a cardinal and gave him important posts. The promotion caused widespread scandal at the time, and Innocenzo's later misconduct deepened it. Julius III died on 23 March 1555.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Maria Ciocchi del Monte in Rome in 1487
Co-presided over the opening of the Council of Trent in 1545
Reconvened the Council of Trent in May 1551
Founded the Collegium Germanicum with St. Ignatius (1552)
England reconciled with Rome under Mary I (1554)
Died 23 March 1555

faqs.question: What role did Julius III play at the Council of Trent?
faqs.answer: As Cardinal del Monte he was a presiding legate at its opening in 1545, and as pope he reconvened it in 1551 until war forced its suspension in 1552.

faqs.question: What was the Collegium Germanicum?
faqs.answer: A Roman seminary founded by Julius III in 1552 at the suggestion of St. Ignatius of Loyola to form priests for Germany and neighboring lands. It still operates as the Collegium Germanicum et Hungaricum.

faqs.question: Who was Innocenzo del Monte?
faqs.answer: A youth adopted by the pope's brother, whom Julius III made a cardinal at about 17. The appointment was widely criticized as an abuse of nepotism, and Innocenzo later fell into disgrace.

directAnswer: Pope Marcellus II was Marcello Cervini, a reform-minded scholar and former legate at the Council of Trent, who reigned for only 22 days in April 1555. He was the last pope to keep his baptismal name, and Palestrina's famous Missa Papae Marcelli bears his name.

sections.h2: Marcello Cervini, Scholar and Reformer
paras: Marcello Cervini was born on 6 May 1501 at Montefano in the Marche, to a family from Montepulciano. A gifted student of languages, mathematics and astronomy, he entered the service of Cardinal Alessandro Farnese and became secretary to Paul III, who made him a cardinal in 1539.

He was one of the presiding legates at the Council of Trent from 1545, where he was known for seriousness and for resisting imperial pressure. He also served as Vatican librarian, expanding its collection of Greek and Latin manuscripts.

sections.h2: Twenty-Two Days and a Lasting Name
paras: Elected on 9 April 1555, Cervini chose to keep his own name, becoming Marcellus II; no pope since has done so. He immediately curtailed the expense of his coronation, forbade relatives to come to Rome seeking favors, and signaled that reform would begin with the papal court itself.

His hopes ended quickly: he suffered a stroke and died on 1 May 1555. Twelve years later Palestrina published the Missa Papae Marcelli in his memory. A later legend claimed this Mass persuaded the Council of Trent not to ban polyphonic music; historians regard that story as an embellishment, though the work did exemplify the clear setting of sacred text that reformers desired.

keyFacts: Born Marcello Cervini at Montefano on 6 May 1501
Presiding legate at the Council of Trent and Vatican librarian
Elected 9 April 1555; died 1 May 1555
Last pope to retain his baptismal name
Honored in Palestrina's Missa Papae Marcelli (published 1567)

faqs.question: Why did Marcellus II keep his own name?
faqs.answer: He chose not to adopt a new papal name, and no pope since has done the same. His reasons are not recorded beyond his personal preference.

faqs.question: Did the Missa Papae Marcelli save church music at Trent?
faqs.answer: That is a later legend. Palestrina's Mass, published in 1567 and dedicated to the memory of Marcellus II, did show that polyphony could keep sacred words intelligible, which was the council's concern.

directAnswer: Pope Paul IV was Gian Pietro Carafa, co-founder of the Theatine order and a leading figure of the Roman Inquisition, who reigned from 1555 to 1559. A severe reformer, he established the Roman Ghetto with the bull Cum nimis absurdum, published the first papal Index of Forbidden Books, and fought a disastrous war against Spain.

sections.h2: Co-Founder of the Theatines
paras: Gian Pietro Carafa was born on 28 June 1476 at Capriglia Irpina near Avellino, in the Kingdom of Naples, into a powerful Neapolitan family. He served as a papal diplomat, including in England and Spain, and became bishop of Chieti, whose Latin name Theate later gave a name to his religious order.

In 1524 he resigned his benefices and joined St. Cajetan of Thiene in founding the Theatines, a community of priests committed to poverty and pastoral reform. Paul III made him a cardinal in 1536, and he served on the 1537 reform commission.

sections.h2: The Inquisition and the Index
paras: Carafa was a principal promoter of the Roman Inquisition established in 1542 and directed it with great severity. Elected pope on 23 May 1555 at nearly 79, he continued that approach, pursuing even respected cardinals such as Giovanni Morone, whom he imprisoned on suspicion of heresy.

In 1559 he published the first Index of Forbidden Books issued by a pope, so sweeping that it was moderated by his successor. He also pressed Michelangelo's Last Judgment as indecent; the covering of its nudes was carried out only after his death.

sections.h2: Cum Nimis Absurdum and the Roman Ghetto
paras: In July 1555 Paul IV issued the bull Cum nimis absurdum, which confined Rome's Jews to a walled quarter near the Tiber, required them to wear a distinguishing sign, and restricted their trades and property. The Roman Ghetto lasted until 1870.

The Church today regards such measures with deep regret. Recent popes have visited Rome's synagogue, which stands near the site of the old ghetto, as a sign of a very different relationship with the Jewish people.

sections.h2: War with Spain and the Fall of the Carafa Nephews
paras: Fiercely hostile to Spanish rule over Naples, Paul IV allied with France against Philip II. In 1556 and 1557 the Duke of Alba's army invaded the Papal States, and the pope was forced to make peace.

His nephew Cardinal Carlo Carafa had driven much of this policy. In 1559 Paul IV discovered his nephews' misconduct, stripped them of office and banished them from Rome. When he died on 18 August 1559, crowds tore down his statue on the Capitol and attacked the offices of the Inquisition.

keyFacts: Born Gian Pietro Carafa at Capriglia Irpina on 28 June 1476
Co-founded the Theatines with St. Cajetan of Thiene (1524)
Issued Cum nimis absurdum establishing the Roman Ghetto (1555)
Published the first papal Index of Forbidden Books (1559)
Fought a losing war against Spain (1556 to 1557)
Died 18 August 1559

faqs.question: What was Cum nimis absurdum?
faqs.answer: A 1555 bull of Paul IV that confined Rome's Jews to a walled ghetto and imposed severe restrictions on them. The ghetto remained until 1870, and the Church now recognizes such measures as grave wrongs.

faqs.question: How are the Theatines connected to Paul IV?
faqs.answer: As Gian Pietro Carafa he co-founded the order with St. Cajetan of Thiene in 1524. The name comes from Theate, the Latin name of Chieti, where Carafa had been bishop.

faqs.question: Did Paul IV have the Last Judgment painted over?
faqs.answer: He objected to its nudity, but the draperies were added by Daniele da Volterra after his death, following a decree of the Council of Trent in 1563.

directAnswer: Pope Pius IV was Giovanni Angelo Medici of Milan, who reigned from 1559 to 1565. He reconvened and brought to a successful close the Council of Trent in 1563, confirmed its decrees, issued the Tridentine Profession of Faith, and relied on his nephew St. Charles Borromeo as his chief collaborator.

sections.h2: A Milanese Lawyer, Not a Florentine Medici
paras: Giovanni Angelo Medici was born in Milan on 31 March 1499. His family was unrelated to the Medici of Florence, though they later claimed a connection. He studied law at Bologna, served as a papal governor of several towns, and was made a cardinal by Paul III in 1549.
Having fallen out of favor under Paul IV, he emerged from a conclave of nearly four months as a conciliatory choice and was elected at the end of December 1559.

sections.h2: Bringing the Council of Trent to Completion
paras: Pius IV's great achievement was the Council of Trent. He reconvened it in January 1562 after a ten-year suspension and guided it through difficult debates about bishops' residence and authority. Cardinal Giovanni Morone, whom Paul IV had imprisoned, was released and became the legate who steered the council to its close on 4 December 1563.

In January 1564 Pius IV confirmed all the decrees with the bull Benedictus Deus. That year he also issued a revised Index of Forbidden Books and the Profession of Faith of the Council of Trent, which clergy and teachers were required to take for centuries afterward.

sections.h2: St. Charles Borromeo at His Side
paras: Pius IV made his young nephew Charles Borromeo a cardinal and archbishop of Milan in 1560 and entrusted him with the daily business of the Holy See. In this case family favor produced a saint; Borromeo became a model of the reforming bishop envisioned by Trent.
By contrast, the pope allowed a trial of Paul IV's nephews, and Cardinal Carlo Carafa and his brother were executed in 1561, a harsh end to that family's power.

sections.h2: Porta Pia, Water, and Building in Rome
paras: Pius IV improved Rome's water supply by restoring the ancient Aqua Virgo and commissioned Michelangelo to design the Porta Pia and to convert part of the Baths of Diocletian into the church of Santa Maria degli Angeli. In the Vatican gardens he completed the elegant Casina Pio IV.
A plot to assassinate him was uncovered in 1565. He died on 9 December 1565, attended by Charles Borromeo.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Angelo Medici in Milan on 31 March 1499
Reconvened the Council of Trent in 1562; it closed on 4 December 1563
Confirmed the council's decrees with Benedictus Deus (1564)
Issued the Tridentine Profession of Faith (1564)
Uncle of St. Charles Borromeo
Commissioned Michelangelo's Porta Pia

faqs.question: Was Pius IV related to the Medici of Florence?
faqs.answer: No. Despite sharing the surname, his Milanese family was not part of the Florentine dynasty.

faqs.question: What did Pius IV do at the Council of Trent?
faqs.answer: He reconvened it in 1562, supported the legates who brought it to a close in December 1563, and formally confirmed its decrees in 1564.

faqs.question: What is the Tridentine Profession of Faith?
faqs.answer: A creed issued by Pius IV in 1564 summarizing Catholic doctrine as taught at Trent. Bishops, clergy and teachers were long required to profess it.

directAnswer: Pope St. Pius V was Antonio Ghislieri, a Dominican friar who reigned from 1566 to 1572. He put the Council of Trent into practice by issuing the Roman Catechism, Breviary and the 1570 Roman Missal, organized the Holy League that won the Battle of Lepanto, and was canonized in 1712.

sections.h2: Brother Michele, Dominican and Inquisitor
paras: Antonio Ghislieri was born on 17 January 1504 at Bosco, near Alessandria in the Duchy of Milan, to a poor family. He entered the Dominican Order at fourteen, taking the name Michele, and taught theology and philosophy before serving as an inquisitor in northern Italy.

Paul IV made him a bishop and, in 1557, a cardinal and appointed him grand inquisitor. Known for austerity and personal holiness, he was elected pope on 7 January 1566 with the strong support of St. Charles Borromeo. He continued to wear his white Dominican habit, which is often cited as the origin of the pope's white cassock.

sections.h2: The Roman Missal and the Reform of Worship
paras: Pius V devoted himself to implementing Trent. He published the Roman Catechism in 1566, the reformed Roman Breviary in 1568, and in July 1570, with the bull Quo primum, the Roman Missal that remained the standard form of the Latin Mass for four centuries.
In 1567 he declared St. Thomas Aquinas a Doctor of the Church. He enforced the residence of bishops, reformed the Curia, cut the expenses of the papal court, and lived simply himself.

sections.h2: Lepanto and Our Lady of Victory
paras: Alarmed by Ottoman expansion, Pius V formed the Holy League with Spain and Venice. On 7 October 1571 its fleet defeated the Ottoman navy at Lepanto off the coast of Greece. The pope had urged the faithful to pray the Rosary for victory.

In thanksgiving he established a feast of Our Lady of Victory, which his successor Gregory XIII renamed the feast of the Holy Rosary. It is still kept on 7 October. Pius V had earlier given papal approval to the form of the Rosary in a 1569 bull.

sections.h2: Regnans in Excelsis and Canonization
paras: In 1570 Pius V issued Regnans in Excelsis, excommunicating Queen Elizabeth I of England and releasing her subjects from allegiance. The bull made life harder for English Catholics, who were increasingly treated as potential traitors.
Pius V died on 1 May 1572 and is buried in the Basilica of St. Mary Major. He was beatified by Clement X in 1672 and canonized by Clement XI in 1712. His feast is celebrated on 30 April.

keyFacts: Born Antonio Ghislieri at Bosco on 17 January 1504; Dominican name Michele
Issued the Roman Catechism (1566), Breviary (1568) and Missal (1570)
Declared St. Thomas Aquinas a Doctor of the Church (1567)
Excommunicated Elizabeth I with Regnans in Excelsis (1570)
Holy League victory at Lepanto on 7 October 1571
Canonized by Clement XI in 1712; feast day 30 April

faqs.question: Why is St. Pius V linked to the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary?
faqs.answer: After the Holy League won at Lepanto on 7 October 1571, a victory for which he had asked the faithful to pray the Rosary, he instituted a feast of Our Lady of Victory. Gregory XIII renamed it the feast of the Holy Rosary.

faqs.question: What is the Missal of Pius V?
faqs.answer: The Roman Missal he promulgated in 1570 with the bull Quo primum. With later revisions it was the standard Mass of the Latin Church until the reforms after the Second Vatican Council.

faqs.question: When was Pius V canonized?
faqs.answer: He was beatified in 1672 by Clement X and canonized on 22 May 1712 by Clement XI.

directAnswer: Pope Gregory XIII was Ugo Boncompagni, a Bolognese canon lawyer who reigned from 1572 to 1585. He introduced the Gregorian calendar in 1582, still used worldwide, and founded or endowed many colleges in Rome, including the Roman College that became the Pontifical Gregorian University.

sections.h2: Ugo Boncompagni, Jurist of Bologna
paras: Ugo Boncompagni was born in Bologna on 7 January 1502. He taught law at the university there, and before his ordination he fathered a son, Giacomo, whom he later provided for. He entered papal service, worked as a canonist at the Council of Trent, and was made a cardinal by Pius IV in 1565.

Elected on 13 May 1572, he committed himself to carrying out the Tridentine reforms. Under the influence of the reformers around him, he lived more austerely as pope than he had earlier in his career.

sections.h2: The Gregorian Calendar of 1582
paras: The Julian calendar had drifted about ten days from the solar year, pushing the date of Easter away from the spring equinox. Drawing on the proposal of Aloysius Lilius and the work of the Jesuit astronomer Christopher Clavius, Gregory XIII issued the bull Inter gravissimas in February 1582.

In Catholic countries Thursday, 4 October 1582, was followed by Friday, 15 October. The reform also refined the leap-year rule so that century years are leap years only when divisible by 400. Protestant and Orthodox lands adopted it more slowly; Britain and its American colonies switched only in 1752.

sections.h2: Colleges, Seminaries, and Missions
paras: Gregory XIII was a great patron of education. He generously endowed the Jesuit Roman College, which took the name Gregorian University in his honor, and founded or supported national colleges in Rome, including the German-Hungarian, English, Greek and Maronite colleges.

He sent nuncios across Europe to promote Trent's decrees and encouraged missions in Asia. In 1585, shortly before his death, he received the first Japanese embassy to Europe, four young Christian nobles sent by Japanese lords. He also issued a revised Roman Martyrology and an official edition of the body of canon law.

sections.h2: St. Bartholomew's Day and Papal Finances
paras: When news arrived of the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of Huguenots in France in 1572, the pope ordered a Te Deum and struck a commemorative medal, having been told of a foiled Protestant plot. The episode is remembered as a dark moment in his reign.

His generosity strained the treasury, and efforts to raise revenue by reclaiming noble estates fed widespread banditry in the Papal States. Gregory XIII died on 10 April 1585 and is buried in the Gregorian Chapel he built in St. Peter's.

keyFacts: Born Ugo Boncompagni in Bologna on 7 January 1502
Introduced the Gregorian calendar with Inter gravissimas (1582)
Endowed the Roman College, now the Pontifical Gregorian University
Founded or supported national colleges in Rome, including the English College
Received the first Japanese embassy to Europe (1585)
Died 10 April 1585

faqs.question: Why did Gregory XIII reform the calendar?
faqs.answer: The Julian calendar had slipped about ten days behind the solar year, disrupting the calculation of Easter. His 1582 reform removed ten days and adjusted the leap-year rule.

faqs.question: Is the Gregorian University named after Gregory XIII?
faqs.answer: Yes. He richly endowed the Jesuit Roman College, which became known as the Gregorian University in recognition of his support.

faqs.question: How did Gregory XIII react to the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre?
faqs.answer: Informed that a Huguenot plot had been foiled, he ordered thanksgiving services and a medal. Historians count this among the troubling episodes of his pontificate.

directAnswer: Pope Sixtus V was Felice Peretti, a Conventual Franciscan of humble birth who reigned from 1585 to 1590. In five energetic years he suppressed banditry, restored papal finances, reshaped Rome with new streets, an aqueduct and obelisks, completed the dome of St. Peter's, fixed the College of Cardinals at 70, and reorganized the Curia into congregations.

sections.h2: Felice Peretti, Franciscan Preacher
paras: Felice Peretti was born on 13 December 1521 at Grottammare in the Marche, to a poor family; as a boy he is said to have tended animals. He joined the Conventual Franciscans, became a celebrated preacher, and served as an inquisitor in Venice, where his severity provoked opposition.

Pius V made him a cardinal in 1570, and he became known as Cardinal Montalto. During the reign of Gregory XIII he lived largely in retirement, editing the works of St. Ambrose. He was elected on 24 April 1585.

sections.h2: Order and Finances in the Papal States
paras: Sixtus V moved swiftly against the banditry that had flourished under his predecessor, enforcing harsh penalties until the roads were safe again. He also restored the treasury, accumulating a large reserve in Castel Sant'Angelo through strict economy, new taxes and the sale of offices.
In 1588 his bull Effraenatam imposed severe canonical penalties for abortion and contraception. He also supported the Catholic League in France and excommunicated Henry of Navarre in 1585.

sections.h2: Remaking Rome: Streets, Obelisks, and the Dome
paras: With his architect Domenico Fontana, Sixtus V planned straight avenues linking Rome's major basilicas, including the Strada Felice. He built the Acqua Felice aqueduct to bring water to the city's hills and in 1586 had the Vatican obelisk moved to the center of St. Peter's Square, followed by obelisks at St. Mary Major, the Lateran and the Piazza del Popolo.
He rebuilt the Lateran Palace, erected the present Vatican Library building, and pushed to completion the dome of St. Peter's following Michelangelo's design, finished by Giacomo della Porta in 1590.

sections.h2: Seventy Cardinals and Fifteen Congregations
paras: In 1586 Sixtus V fixed the maximum number of cardinals at 70, a limit that held until the twentieth century. In 1588 his constitution Immensa aeterni Dei organized the Curia into fifteen permanent congregations of cardinals, each with its own area of responsibility, a structure that shaped Church government for centuries.

He declared St. Bonaventure a Doctor of the Church in 1588 and issued an edition of the Latin Vulgate in 1590, which was withdrawn after his death because of its errors. Sixtus V died on 27 August 1590.

keyFacts: Born Felice Peretti at Grottammare on 13 December 1521
Conventual Franciscan friar; cardinal from 1570
Limited the College of Cardinals to 70 (1586)
Created fifteen Curial congregations with Immensa aeterni Dei (1588)
Raised the obelisk in St. Peter's Square (1586) and completed the dome (1590)
Declared St. Bonaventure a Doctor of the Church (1588)

faqs.question: Why did Sixtus V limit the College of Cardinals to 70?
faqs.answer: In 1586 he set the maximum at 70, recalling the seventy elders who assisted Moses. The limit remained until John XXIII exceeded it in 1958.

faqs.question: Who put the obelisk in St. Peter's Square?
faqs.answer: Sixtus V had his engineer Domenico Fontana move the ancient Egyptian obelisk to the square's center in 1586, a celebrated feat of engineering.

faqs.question: What happened to the Sixtine Vulgate?
faqs.answer: His 1590 edition of the Latin Bible contained many errors and was withdrawn after his death. A corrected Sixto-Clementine Vulgate appeared under Clement VIII in 1592.

directAnswer: Pope Urban VII was Giovanni Battista Castagna, a Roman-born diplomat elected on 15 September 1590 who died of malaria just 13 days later, before he could be crowned. His is the shortest pontificate in history.

sections.h2: Giovanni Battista Castagna, Diplomat of Trent
paras: Giovanni Battista Castagna was born in Rome on 4 August 1521 to a Genoese family. Trained in law, he became archbishop of Rossano in Calabria in 1553, took part in the Council of Trent, and served as papal nuncio to Spain for several years and as governor in the Papal States.

Gregory XIII created him a cardinal in 1583. He also served the Inquisition. When the conclave met after Sixtus V's death, Castagna was elected on 15 September 1590 with Spanish backing and took the name Urban VII.

sections.h2: Thirteen Days
paras: Accounts of his brief reign describe a pope concerned for Rome's poor, who ordered economies in the papal court. He is also credited with a decree forbidding tobacco use in or near churches, often cited as one of the earliest public smoking bans.

Urban VII contracted malaria and died on 27 September 1590, before his coronation. He left his considerable fortune to a Roman confraternity to provide dowries for poor young women. He is buried in Santa Maria sopra Minerva. Beyond these details, his reign was too short to leave a lasting mark.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Battista Castagna in Rome on 4 August 1521
Archbishop of Rossano and participant at the Council of Trent
Papal nuncio to Spain; cardinal from 1583
Elected 15 September 1590; died 27 September 1590
Shortest pontificate in history; never crowned

faqs.question: Which pope had the shortest reign?
faqs.answer: Urban VII, who died of malaria 13 days after his election in September 1590, before his coronation.

faqs.question: Did Urban VII ban smoking?
faqs.answer: He is credited with forbidding tobacco use in and around churches, a decree often described as one of the first smoking bans, though details of its enforcement are scarce.

directAnswer: Pope Gregory XIV was Niccolo Sfondrati, a Lombard bishop and friend of St. Charles Borromeo, who reigned from December 1590 to October 1591. His short pontificate is remembered for strong support of the Catholic League against Henry of Navarre, a bull forbidding betting on papal elections, and the softening of Sixtus V's penalties on abortion.

sections.h2: Bishop of Cremona and Friend of Borromeo
paras: Niccolo Sfondrati was born on 11 February 1535 at Somma Lombardo, near Milan, the son of a senator who later became a cardinal. He studied law, became bishop of Cremona in 1560, and took part in the final sessions of the Council of Trent.

A close friend of St. Charles Borromeo and of St. Philip Neri, he was known for personal piety and simplicity. Gregory XIII made him a cardinal in 1583. After a two-month conclave dominated by Spanish influence, he was elected on 5 December 1590.

sections.h2: The Catholic League and Henry of Navarre
paras: France was then torn by the Wars of Religion. Gregory XIV renewed the excommunication of the Protestant Henry of Navarre, heir to the French throne, and sent money and troops under his nephew Ercole Sfondrati to aid the Catholic League. The expedition achieved little.
His nephew Paolo Emilio Sfondrati, whom he made a cardinal, took over much of the administration, and the pope's frequent illness left him limited capacity to govern personally.

sections.h2: Cogit Nos and Sedes Apostolica
paras: In 1591 Gregory XIV issued the bull Cogit nos, forbidding wagers on the outcome of papal elections, the length of a pontificate or the creation of cardinals, under pain of excommunication. Betting on conclaves had become a popular pastime among Roman bankers and merchants.

In the same year his constitution Sedes Apostolica modified the severe penalties of Sixtus V's Effraenatam, restricting the reserved excommunication for abortion to cases after the fetus was considered animated, following the medieval distinction then current, and dropping it for contraception. During his reign Rome also endured famine and plague. Gregory XIV died on 16 October 1591.

keyFacts: Born Niccolo Sfondrati at Somma Lombardo on 11 February 1535
Bishop of Cremona and participant at the Council of Trent
Friend of St. Charles Borromeo and St. Philip Neri
Supported the Catholic League against Henry of Navarre
Banned betting on papal elections with Cogit nos (1591)
Died 16 October 1591

faqs.question: Why did Gregory XIV ban betting on papal elections?
faqs.answer: Wagering on conclaves and the creation of cardinals had become common in Rome. His 1591 bull Cogit nos made such bets punishable by excommunication to protect the dignity of the election.

faqs.question: How did Gregory XIV change Sixtus V's law on abortion?
faqs.answer: His 1591 constitution Sedes Apostolica limited the special excommunication to abortion of an ensouled fetus, as theologians of the time understood it, and removed it for contraception. The Church's moral teaching that abortion is gravely wrong was not changed.

directAnswer: Pope Innocent IX was Giovanni Antonio Facchinetti of Bologna, a veteran diplomat and canonist who reigned for two months, from 29 October to 30 December 1591. He supported Spain and the Catholic League in the French Wars of Religion and forbade the alienation of Church property before illness ended his reign.

sections.h2: A Career in Papal Diplomacy
paras: Giovanni Antonio Facchinetti was born in Bologna on 20 July 1519. After studying law, he served Cardinal Alessandro Farnese, became bishop of Nicastro in Calabria in 1560, and attended the Council of Trent.

As nuncio to Venice under Pius V, he helped prepare the alliance that fought at Lepanto. He was named titular Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem and was created a cardinal by Gregory XIII in 1583, later serving on the Inquisition. Spanish support helped elect him on 29 October 1591.

sections.h2: Two Months on the Throne of Peter
paras: Innocent IX was already elderly and in poor health. In his few weeks he continued his predecessor's backing of Philip II of Spain and the Catholic League against Henry IV of France, prohibited the alienation of Church property, and took steps against banditry.

Sources also describe him reorganizing the work of the Secretariat of State into sections by region, though details are sparse. He died on 30 December 1591, scarcely two months after his election. Little else is recorded of his short reign.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Antonio Facchinetti in Bologna on 20 July 1519
Bishop of Nicastro and participant at the Council of Trent
Nuncio to Venice during preparations for Lepanto
Elected 29 October 1591; died 30 December 1591
Prohibited the alienation of Church property

faqs.question: How long did Innocent IX reign?
faqs.answer: About two months, from his election on 29 October 1591 until his death on 30 December 1591.

faqs.question: What side did Innocent IX take in the French Wars of Religion?
faqs.answer: Like Gregory XIV, he supported Philip II of Spain and the Catholic League against the Protestant claimant Henry IV.

directAnswer: Pope Clement VIII was Ippolito Aldobrandini, who reigned from 1592 to 1605. He reconciled King Henry IV of France to the Church in 1595, issued the corrected Sixto-Clementine Vulgate, annexed Ferrara to the Papal States, celebrated the Jubilee of 1600, and convened the Congregatio de Auxiliis on the debate over grace and free will.

sections.h2: Ippolito Aldobrandini, Lawyer and Legate to Poland
paras: Ippolito Aldobrandini was born at Fano on 24 February 1536, into a Florentine family exiled by the Medici. He trained in law and held offices in the Roman tribunals before Sixtus V made him a cardinal in 1585.

As papal legate to Poland in 1588 he negotiated the release of Archduke Maximilian of Austria, captured in a disputed royal election, which earned him the gratitude of the Habsburgs. Elected on 30 January 1592, he was known for intense personal piety and spent long hours in prayer and confession; the historian Caesar Baronius served as his confessor.

sections.h2: The Absolution of Henry IV
paras: Clement VIII's most consequential decision concerned France. Henry of Navarre, the Protestant heir, had converted to Catholicism in 1593. Despite strong Spanish objections, Clement formally absolved him in September 1595, recognizing him as king.

The reconciliation helped end the French Wars of Religion and restored the balance between France and Spain in papal diplomacy. In 1598 Clement also secured the duchy of Ferrara for the Papal States after the Este line failed.

sections.h2: The Vulgate, the Liturgy, and the Union of Brest
paras: In 1592 Clement VIII issued the corrected Latin Bible known as the Sixto-Clementine Vulgate, which remained the official Latin text of the Catholic Church until the twentieth century. He also published revised editions of the Pontifical, the Breviary and the Missal, and a new Index of Forbidden Books in 1596.

In 1595 and 1596 bishops of the Ruthenian Church in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth entered communion with Rome while keeping their Byzantine liturgy, an agreement known as the Union of Brest. Clement created influential cardinals, among them Baronius and Robert Bellarmine.

sections.h2: Grace, the Ottomans, and the Jubilee of 1600
paras: In 1597 Clement VIII set up the Congregatio de Auxiliis to resolve a bitter dispute between Dominicans and Jesuits about how divine grace works with human freedom. The commission met for years without a final ruling, and Paul V later allowed both schools to continue teaching.

Clement supported the Habsburg war against the Ottoman Empire known as the Long War, sending troops and funds to Hungary. The Jubilee of 1600 drew enormous crowds to Rome. That same year the philosopher Giordano Bruno was burned in the Campo de' Fiori after a long trial by the Roman Inquisition, an event the Church has since acknowledged with regret. Clement VIII died on 3 March 1605.

keyFacts: Born Ippolito Aldobrandini at Fano on 24 February 1536
Absolved and recognized Henry IV of France (1595)
Issued the Sixto-Clementine Vulgate (1592)
Annexed Ferrara to the Papal States (1598)
Union of Brest with the Ruthenian Church (1595 to 1596)
Convened the Congregatio de Auxiliis (1597)

faqs.question: Why did Clement VIII absolve Henry IV?
faqs.answer: Henry had converted to Catholicism in 1593. Clement accepted his conversion in 1595 despite Spanish opposition, which helped bring peace to France after decades of religious war.

faqs.question: What was the Congregatio de Auxiliis?
faqs.answer: A papal commission begun in 1597 to settle a Dominican and Jesuit dispute about grace and free will. It ended under Paul V without a definitive decision, both views being permitted.

faqs.question: What is the Sixto-Clementine Vulgate?
faqs.answer: The corrected official Latin Bible published by Clement VIII in 1592, replacing the faulty edition of Sixtus V. It served as the Church's standard Latin text for centuries.

directAnswer: Pope Leo XI was Alessandro Ottaviano de' Medici, archbishop of Florence and a great-nephew of Leo X, who reigned for just 27 days in April 1605. His brief pontificate earned him the Italian nickname Papa Lampo, the Lightning Pope.

sections.h2: A Medici Disciple of St. Philip Neri
paras: Alessandro Ottaviano de' Medici was born in Florence on 2 June 1535. Through his mother, a granddaughter of Lorenzo the Magnificent, he was a great-nephew of Pope Leo X. He felt drawn to the priesthood from youth, though his family's ambitions delayed his ordination.

In Rome he became a close friend and spiritual follower of St. Philip Neri. He served for years as the Tuscan ambassador to the Holy See, became archbishop of Florence in 1574, and was created a cardinal by Gregory XIII in 1583.

sections.h2: Legate to France and the Lightning Pope
paras: After Clement VIII absolved Henry IV, Cardinal de' Medici served as papal legate to France from 1596 to 1598, a period that included the negotiation of the Peace of Vervins between France and Spain. This made him a favorite of the French court, which supported his candidacy in 1605.

Elected on 1 April 1605 at the age of 69, he took the name Leo in honor of his great-uncle. Soon afterward he caught a chill, reportedly during the ceremony of taking possession of the Lateran, and he died on 27 April 1605. His tomb in St. Peter's, by Alessandro Algardi, was completed decades later. Little else from his reign is recorded.

keyFacts: Born Alessandro Ottaviano de' Medici in Florence on 2 June 1535
Great-nephew of Pope Leo X; follower of St. Philip Neri
Archbishop of Florence from 1574; cardinal from 1583
Papal legate to France (1596 to 1598)
Reigned 1 to 27 April 1605; nicknamed Papa Lampo

faqs.question: Why is Leo XI called the Lightning Pope?
faqs.answer: Because his pontificate lasted only 27 days in April 1605, Italians nicknamed him Papa Lampo, meaning lightning pope.

faqs.question: How was Leo XI related to Leo X?
faqs.answer: His mother was a granddaughter of Lorenzo the Magnificent, making him a great-nephew of Leo X, whose papal name he chose.

directAnswer: Pope Paul V was Camillo Borghese, a Roman canon lawyer who reigned from 1605 to 1621. He completed the nave and facade of St. Peter's Basilica, built the Acqua Paola aqueduct, founded the Vatican Secret Archives, faced down Venice in the Interdict of 1606, and presided over the 1616 decision against Copernican teaching.

sections.h2: Camillo Borghese, Canonist and Cardinal Vicar
paras: Camillo Borghese was born in Rome on 17 September 1550 to a family of Sienese origin. He studied law at Perugia and Padua, held posts in the Curia, and went on a diplomatic mission to Spain. Clement VIII made him a cardinal in 1596 and later cardinal vicar of Rome.

Considered a neutral figure between the French and Spanish factions, he was elected on 16 May 1605 after the death of Leo XI. As pope he insisted firmly on the rights of the Church as defined by canon law.

sections.h2: The Venetian Interdict of 1606
paras: When the Republic of Venice passed laws restricting Church property and tried clergy in civil courts, Paul V placed the city under interdict in 1606. Venice, defended in print by the Servite friar Paolo Sarpi, ordered its clergy to ignore the sanction, and the Jesuits and some other orders were expelled.
French mediation ended the dispute in 1607 without a clear victory for either side. In 1606 Paul V also condemned the oath of allegiance required of English Catholics after the Gunpowder Plot.

sections.h2: Galileo and the Decree of 1616
paras: In 1616 the Congregation of the Index suspended Copernicus's book on the motion of the earth until corrected, and Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, at the pope's direction, instructed Galileo not to hold or defend the heliocentric view as proven. Galileo complied for the time being.
The decision set the stage for Galileo's trial in 1633 under Urban VIII. In 1992 St. John Paul II acknowledged that the theologians of the time had erred in their judgment.

sections.h2: St. Peter's Facade, Acqua Paola, and the Archives
paras: Paul V commissioned Carlo Maderno to extend the nave of St. Peter's and build its facade, completed in 1612 and still inscribed with his name. He restored the ancient Aqua Traiana as the Acqua Paola, with its monumental fountain on the Janiculum, and built the Pauline Chapel in St. Mary Major.

In 1612 he gathered papal records into what became the Vatican Secret Archives, now called the Vatican Apostolic Archive, and in 1605 he founded the Bank of the Holy Spirit. He canonized St. Charles Borromeo in 1610, issued the Roman Ritual in 1614, and received a Japanese embassy led by Hasekura Tsunenaga in 1615. His nephew Cardinal Scipione Borghese built the Villa Borghese. Paul V died on 28 January 1621.

keyFacts: Born Camillo Borghese in Rome on 17 September 1550
Placed Venice under interdict (1606 to 1607)
Completed the facade of St. Peter's Basilica (1612)
Founded the Vatican Secret Archives (1612)
Canonized St. Charles Borromeo (1610); issued the Roman Ritual (1614)
Died 28 January 1621

faqs.question: Whose name is on the facade of St. Peter's Basilica?
faqs.answer: Paul V's. The inscription across Carlo Maderno's facade, finished in 1612, names Paul V Borghese as its builder.

faqs.question: What was the Venetian Interdict?
faqs.answer: In 1606 Paul V placed Venice under interdict over laws limiting Church property and clerical immunity. Venice resisted, and France mediated a settlement in 1607.

faqs.question: What role did Paul V play in the Galileo affair?
faqs.answer: Under his pontificate in 1616 Copernicus's work was suspended and Galileo was told not to defend heliocentrism. The later trial took place under Urban VIII.

directAnswer: Pope Gregory XV was Alessandro Ludovisi of Bologna, who reigned from 1621 to 1623. In just over two years he established the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith to direct Catholic missions, required secret written ballots in papal conclaves, and canonized Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Avila, Philip Neri and Isidore the Farmer on a single day.

sections.h2: Alessandro Ludovisi, Jesuit-Trained Archbishop
