paras: Alessandro Ludovisi was born in Bologna on 9 January 1554 and educated by the Jesuits at the Roman College before studying law. He served as a judge in Rome, became archbishop of Bologna in 1612, and was created a cardinal by Paul V in 1616.
Elected on 9 February 1621 at 67 and in frail health, he relied heavily on his capable nephew Ludovico Ludovisi, whom he made a cardinal immediately.

sections.h2: Reforming the Conclave
paras: Gregory XV's bull Aeterni Patris Filius of 1621 required that popes be elected by secret written ballot, replacing elections by acclamation or open agreement that had allowed pressure and bargaining. A further constitution in 1622 regulated conclave ceremonies.
These rules gave the modern conclave much of its shape, and later legislation, including that of the twentieth century, built on them.

sections.h2: Propaganda Fide and the Great Canonization of 1622
paras: On 6 January 1622, with the bull Inscrutabili Divinae, Gregory XV established the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, known as Propaganda Fide, to coordinate missions throughout the world and reduce dependence on the colonial powers. It remains a central office of the Holy See under the Dicastery for Evangelization.

On 12 March 1622 he canonized Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Avila, Philip Neri and Isidore the Farmer, a celebrated ceremony that honored the saints of the Catholic Reformation. That year he also raised Paris to an archdiocese.

sections.h2: The Thirty Years' War and the Palatine Library
paras: Gregory XV sent financial support to the Emperor and the Catholic League in the early years of the Thirty Years' War. After the capture of Heidelberg, Duke Maximilian of Bavaria presented the pope with the Palatine Library, whose manuscripts were brought to the Vatican.
In 1623 his constitution Omnipotentis Dei set severe penalties for sorcery and witchcraft. Gregory XV died on 8 July 1623.

keyFacts: Born Alessandro Ludovisi in Bologna on 9 January 1554
Required secret written ballots in conclaves with Aeterni Patris Filius (1621)
Founded the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith (6 January 1622)
Canonized Ignatius, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Avila, Philip Neri and Isidore (12 March 1622)
Received the Palatine Library from Maximilian of Bavaria
Died 8 July 1623

faqs.question: What is Propaganda Fide?
faqs.answer: The Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, founded by Gregory XV in 1622 to direct the Church's worldwide missions. Its work continues today within the Dicastery for Evangelization.

faqs.question: Which saints did Gregory XV canonize in 1622?
faqs.answer: On 12 March 1622 he canonized Ignatius of Loyola, Francis Xavier, Teresa of Avila, Philip Neri and Isidore the Farmer.

faqs.question: How did Gregory XV change papal elections?
faqs.answer: His 1621 bull Aeterni Patris Filius made the secret written ballot the required method of electing a pope.

directAnswer: Pope Urban VIII was Maffeo Barberini of Florence, who reigned from 1623 to 1644. A poet and patron of Bernini, he consecrated the new St. Peter's Basilica in 1626, founded the Urban College, and reformed canonization procedures, but his pontificate is also remembered for the 1633 trial of Galileo and costly nepotism.

sections.h2: Maffeo Barberini, Poet and Diplomat
paras: Maffeo Barberini was born in Florence in April 1568 to a wealthy merchant family and educated by the Jesuits. He became a skilled Latin poet, served as papal nuncio in France, and was made a cardinal by Paul V in 1606.
Elected on 6 August 1623 at 55, he brought great energy to the papacy. His family emblem of bees appears throughout Rome on the buildings and monuments he sponsored.

sections.h2: Bernini and the Consecration of St. Peter's
paras: Urban VIII consecrated the completed St. Peter's Basilica on 18 November 1626. He commissioned Gian Lorenzo Bernini to create the bronze baldacchino over the papal altar and built the Palazzo Barberini. Bronze taken from the Pantheon portico for his projects prompted a famous Roman quip: what the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.
He made Castel Gandolfo a papal summer residence and founded the Urban College in 1627 to train missionary priests for Propaganda Fide.

sections.h2: The Trial of Galileo
paras: As a cardinal Barberini had admired Galileo, and as pope he allowed him to write about the Copernican system so long as he presented it as a hypothesis. Galileo's Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems, published in 1632, was seen as defending heliocentrism and as mocking the pope's own argument.

In 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried Galileo, who abjured and spent his remaining years under house arrest near Florence. The Church later recognized the error; in 1992 John Paul II formally acknowledged that Galileo's judges had been mistaken.

sections.h2: Canonization Rules, Jansenism, and the War of Castro
paras: Urban VIII reformed the process for making saints, requiring careful investigation and forbidding public cult of persons not yet beatified. He revised the Breviary, reduced the number of holy days of obligation in 1642, and in 1624 approved a ban on tobacco in the churches of Seville. In 1642 his bull In eminenti condemned the Jansenist book Augustinus.

His nephews Francesco and Antonio Barberini became cardinals and the family grew immensely rich. The War of Castro against the Farnese duke of Parma, from 1641 to 1644, ended in failure and left the treasury heavily indebted. Urban VIII died on 29 July 1644.

keyFacts: Born Maffeo Barberini in Florence in 1568
Consecrated the new St. Peter's Basilica on 18 November 1626
Commissioned Bernini's baldacchino in St. Peter's
Galileo tried by the Roman Inquisition (1633)
Founded the Urban College for missionaries (1627)
Died 29 July 1644

faqs.question: Why did Urban VIII turn against Galileo?
faqs.answer: He had permitted Galileo to discuss Copernicus as a hypothesis, but the 1632 Dialogue was read as advocating heliocentrism and ridiculing the pope's argument. The Inquisition tried Galileo in 1633.

faqs.question: What did Bernini create for Urban VIII?
faqs.answer: Most famously the bronze baldacchino over the high altar of St. Peter's, along with the Barberini Palace work and Urban's own tomb in the basilica.

faqs.question: How did Urban VIII change canonizations?
faqs.answer: His decrees required thorough investigation of candidates and forbade public veneration of anyone not yet beatified or canonized by the Holy See.

directAnswer: Pope Innocent X was Giovanni Battista Pamphilj, a Roman jurist and diplomat who reigned from 1644 to 1655. He condemned five propositions of Jansenism in the constitution Cum occasione, protested the Peace of Westphalia, and transformed Piazza Navona with Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers and Borromini's Sant'Agnese.

sections.h2: Giovanni Battista Pamphilj, Nuncio to Spain
paras: Giovanni Battista Pamphilj was born in Rome on 6 May 1574 to a family from Gubbio. He studied law, served as a judge of the Roman Rota, and was nuncio in Naples and then Spain. Urban VIII made him a cardinal in 1629.

Elected on 15 September 1644 with Spanish support, he reacted against the Barberini, prosecuting the nephews of Urban VIII for misuse of funds; they fled to France until the French court secured a reconciliation.

sections.h2: Westphalia and Cum Occasione
paras: The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War but confirmed losses of Church lands and rights in the Empire. Innocent X protested the treaty in the brief Zelo domus Dei, declaring its articles harmful to the Church null; the powers ignored it.

On 31 May 1653 his constitution Cum occasione condemned five propositions on grace drawn from Cornelius Jansen's Augustinus as heretical. The decision began a long struggle with the Jansenist party in France.

sections.h2: Piazza Navona and the Jubilee of 1650
paras: Innocent X made Piazza Navona, where his family palace stood, a showpiece of Baroque Rome. Bernini designed the Fountain of the Four Rivers, finished in 1651, and Borromini rebuilt the church of Sant'Agnese in Agone. Velazquez painted his famous portrait of the pope in 1650.
He presided over the Jubilee of 1650 and restored the Lateran Basilica for the occasion. In 1649, during a dispute with the Farnese, his forces destroyed the town of Castro.

sections.h2: Donna Olimpia and the Final Years
paras: His sister-in-law Olimpia Maidalchini exercised unusual influence at his court, which contemporaries resented and satirists exploited. Historians agree her role weakened the reputation of his government, although accounts of her power were sometimes exaggerated.
Innocent X died on 7 January 1655. Reports that his body went unattended for days, with no relative willing to pay for his burial, suggest how isolated he had become at the end.

keyFacts: Born Giovanni Battista Pamphilj in Rome on 6 May 1574
Former nuncio to Naples and Spain; cardinal from 1629
Protested the Peace of Westphalia (1648)
Condemned five Jansenist propositions in Cum occasione (1653)
Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers completed (1651)
Died 7 January 1655

faqs.question: What did Cum occasione condemn?
faqs.answer: Five propositions on divine grace associated with Cornelius Jansen's book Augustinus, which Innocent X declared heretical in 1653.

faqs.question: Why did Innocent X oppose the Peace of Westphalia?
faqs.answer: The treaties confirmed the loss of Church properties and rights in the Empire. He protested them as invalid, but the European powers disregarded the protest.

faqs.question: Who painted the famous portrait of Innocent X?
faqs.answer: Diego Velazquez painted it in Rome in 1650. It hangs in the Doria Pamphilj Gallery.

directAnswer: Pope Alexander VII was Fabio Chigi of Siena, a diplomat and former secretary of state who reigned from 1655 to 1667. He commissioned Bernini's colonnade around St. Peter's Square and the Chair of St. Peter, welcomed the convert Queen Christina of Sweden to Rome, and in 1661 issued Sollicitudo omnium Ecclesiarum defending belief in the Immaculate Conception.

sections.h2: Fabio Chigi, Diplomat at Westphalia
paras: Fabio Chigi was born in Siena on 13 February 1599 to the family of the Renaissance banker Agostino Chigi. As papal nuncio in Cologne he represented the Holy See at the negotiations leading to the Peace of Westphalia and refused to sign treaties that harmed the Church.

Innocent X made him secretary of state and a cardinal in 1652. Elected on 7 April 1655, he at first kept his relatives away from Rome, but within a year he allowed them to come and gave them positions.

sections.h2: Bernini's St. Peter's Square
paras: Alexander VII commissioned Bernini to design the great colonnade enclosing St. Peter's Square, begun in 1656, whose two curving arms embrace pilgrims. Inside the basilica Bernini created the Cathedra Petri, the monumental bronze setting for the ancient chair of St. Peter, and the Scala Regia staircase into the Vatican Palace.

The pope also sponsored churches, streets and squares throughout Rome, including improvements to Piazza del Popolo and the Pantheon area. When plague struck Rome in 1656, his government imposed strict quarantine measures, which are credited with limiting the death toll.

sections.h2: Queen Christina and the Immaculate Conception
paras: In December 1655 Alexander VII welcomed Queen Christina of Sweden to Rome. The daughter of the Protestant champion Gustavus Adolphus had given up her throne and become a Catholic, and he personally confirmed her.

On 8 December 1661 his constitution Sollicitudo omnium Ecclesiarum affirmed the ancient belief that Mary was preserved from original sin from the first moment of her conception and forbade attacks on it. Pius IX drew on this text when defining the dogma in 1854.

sections.h2: Jansenism and Louis XIV
paras: Alexander VII confirmed his predecessor's condemnation of Jansenism and in 1665 required French clergy to sign a formulary accepting it. He canonized St. Francis de Sales the same year.

Relations with Louis XIV were tense. After a brawl in 1662 between the pope's Corsican Guard and the French ambassador's retinue, Louis seized Avignon and forced the humiliating Treaty of Pisa in 1664. Alexander VII died on 22 May 1667.

keyFacts: Born Fabio Chigi in Siena on 13 February 1599
Papal representative at the Westphalia negotiations
Commissioned Bernini's colonnade of St. Peter's Square (begun 1656)
Confirmed Queen Christina of Sweden in Rome (1655)
Issued Sollicitudo omnium Ecclesiarum on the Immaculate Conception (1661)
Canonized St. Francis de Sales (1665)

faqs.question: Did Alexander VII build St. Peter's Square?
faqs.answer: Yes. He commissioned Bernini's elliptical colonnade, begun in 1656, which gives the square its famous embracing form.

faqs.question: What did Alexander VII teach about the Immaculate Conception?
faqs.answer: In 1661 he affirmed that Mary was preserved from original sin from the first instant of her conception and protected that belief from attack. Pius IX later defined it as dogma.

faqs.question: Who was Queen Christina and why did she come to Rome?
faqs.answer: The former queen of Sweden, daughter of Gustavus Adolphus, abdicated and became Catholic. Alexander VII received her in Rome in 1655, where she lived until her death.

directAnswer: Pope Clement IX was Giulio Rospigliosi of Pistoia, a diplomat and opera librettist who reigned from 1667 to 1669. He helped mediate the Peace of Aachen in 1668, arranged a temporary settlement with the Jansenists, and commissioned Bernini's angels for the Ponte Sant'Angelo; the fall of Candia to the Ottomans is said to have hastened his death.

sections.h2: Giulio Rospigliosi, Librettist and Nuncio
paras: Giulio Rospigliosi was born in Pistoia on 28 January 1600 and studied with the Jesuits and at Pisa. In Rome he became a literary figure in the Barberini circle and wrote librettos for early operas, including Sant'Alessio and Chi soffre speri, often counted among the first comic operas.
He served as nuncio to Spain for nearly ten years and then as secretary of state under Alexander VII, who made him a cardinal in 1657. He was elected on 20 June 1667.

sections.h2: Peace of Aachen and the Clementine Peace
paras: Clement IX worked to restore good relations with France and Spain. His diplomacy helped bring about the Peace of Aachen in 1668, ending the War of Devolution between Louis XIV and Spain.

He also arranged the so-called Clementine Peace of 1668 and 1669, under which four French bishops who had resisted the anti-Jansenist formulary signed it with a respectful silence on certain points. The compromise brought a decade of calm to the dispute.

sections.h2: Charity, Saints, and the Angels of Ponte Sant'Angelo
paras: Clement IX lived modestly, gave generously to the poor, and avoided enriching his family; his reported motto described him as clement to others but not to himself. He beatified Rose of Lima in 1668 and canonized Peter of Alcantara and Mary Magdalene de' Pazzi in 1669.

He commissioned Bernini and his workshop to create the ten marble angels bearing the instruments of the Passion that line the Ponte Sant'Angelo, installed around the end of his reign and early in his successor's.

sections.h2: The Fall of Candia
paras: Clement IX sent money and ships to help Venice defend Candia, on Crete, which the Ottomans had besieged for more than twenty years. A French expedition he encouraged failed, and Candia surrendered in September 1669.
Contemporaries believed the loss broke his health. He died on 9 December 1669 and is buried in St. Mary Major.

keyFacts: Born Giulio Rospigliosi in Pistoia on 28 January 1600
Wrote opera librettos, including Chi soffre speri
Helped mediate the Peace of Aachen (1668)
Arranged the Clementine Peace with French Jansenist bishops
Beatified St. Rose of Lima (1668)
Died 9 December 1669; buried in St. Mary Major

faqs.question: Was Clement IX really an opera writer?
faqs.answer: Yes. Before his election, Giulio Rospigliosi wrote librettos for Roman operas in the 1630s and 1640s, including Chi soffre speri, considered one of the earliest comic operas.

faqs.question: Who commissioned the angels on Ponte Sant'Angelo?
faqs.answer: Clement IX commissioned Bernini's workshop to carve the ten angels holding instruments of the Passion. They were installed around 1669 to 1671.

faqs.question: What was the Clementine Peace?
faqs.answer: A 1668 to 1669 compromise in which French bishops sympathetic to Jansenism signed the required formulary, ending open conflict over Jansenism for about a decade.

directAnswer: Pope Clement X was Emilio Altieri, a Roman elected at nearly 80 who reigned from 1670 to 1676. He canonized St. Rose of Lima, the first canonized saint of the Americas, in 1671, beatified Pius V, celebrated the Jubilee of 1675, and supported Poland against the Ottomans, while relying heavily on his adopted cardinal-nephew Paluzzo Altieri.

sections.h2: Emilio Altieri, Elected at Nearly Eighty
paras: Emilio Altieri was born in Rome on 13 July 1590 to an old Roman noble family. He served as a papal official in several posts, including nuncio in Naples and bishop of Camerino, and was made a cardinal by Clement IX only in November 1669, weeks before that pope's death.

The conclave that followed lasted more than four months. Elected on 29 April 1670 at 79, he took the name Clement in honor of his predecessor. Having no nephews of his own, he adopted Cardinal Paluzzo Paluzzi degli Albertoni, who took the name Altieri and effectively ran much of the government.

sections.h2: St. Rose of Lima and the Saints of 1671
paras: On 12 April 1671 Clement X canonized Rose of Lima, the Dominican tertiary of Peru, making her the first saint of the Americas to be canonized. The same ceremony raised Cajetan of Thiene, Francis Borgia, Philip Benizi and Louis Bertrand to the altars.
In 1672 he beatified his Dominican predecessor Pius V. He also issued regulations on the removal of relics from the Roman catacombs.

sections.h2: The Jubilee of 1675 and Sobieski
paras: Clement X presided over the Holy Year of 1675. Bernini's angels on the Ponte Sant'Angelo, begun under Clement IX, were completed early in his reign, and a second fountain was added to St. Peter's Square to balance the first.

Alarmed by Ottoman advances, he sent subsidies to Poland, and the Polish commander John Sobieski won a major victory at Khotyn in 1673 before becoming king. Clement X also faced the opening of Louis XIV's dispute over royal rights to Church revenues. He died on 22 July 1676.

keyFacts: Born Emilio Altieri in Rome on 13 July 1590
Elected 29 April 1670 at age 79
Canonized St. Rose of Lima, first canonized saint of the Americas (1671)
Beatified Pope Pius V (1672)
Celebrated the Jubilee of 1675
Died 22 July 1676

faqs.question: Which pope canonized St. Rose of Lima?
faqs.answer: Clement X, on 12 April 1671. She was the first person from the Americas to be canonized.

faqs.question: Who was Cardinal Paluzzo Altieri?
faqs.answer: A relative by marriage whom the childless and nephewless Clement X adopted into the Altieri family. He became cardinal-nephew and managed much of the pope's government.

faqs.question: How did Clement X respond to the Ottoman threat?
faqs.answer: He sent financial aid to Poland, whose general John Sobieski defeated the Ottomans at Khotyn in 1673.

directAnswer: Blessed Innocent XI was Benedetto Odescalchi of Como, who reigned from 1676 to 1689. A reformer of papal finances and an opponent of nepotism, he condemned laxist moral propositions, resisted Louis XIV's Gallicanism, and organized and financed the alliance that relieved Vienna in 1683. Pius XII beatified him in 1956.

sections.h2: Benedetto Odescalchi of Como
paras: Benedetto Odescalchi was born in Como on 19 May 1611 to a merchant family. After studying law, he entered papal service, was made a cardinal by Innocent X in 1645, and served as legate in Ferrara and then bishop of Novara, earning a reputation for charity during a famine and for simple living.

Elected on 21 September 1676, he took the name Innocent. He refused to enrich his relatives, cut the expenses of the court, and restored order to the papal finances, which had been burdened by debt for decades.

sections.h2: Moral Theology and Catechesis
paras: In 1679 Innocent XI condemned 65 propositions of lax moral theology, including the abuse of mental reservation as a way to deceive under oath. He encouraged frequent Communion and better catechetical instruction of the faithful.
In 1687 he condemned the quietist teaching of the Spanish priest Miguel de Molinos, who held that perfection lay in total passivity of the soul.

sections.h2: Gallicanism and Louis XIV
paras: Innocent XI clashed with Louis XIV over the king's extension of royal rights to the revenues of vacant dioceses. In 1682 the French clergy adopted the Four Gallican Articles limiting papal authority, and the pope refused to confirm bishops who had taken part, leaving many French sees vacant.

He also abolished the abuse of diplomatic quarters in Rome, which sheltered criminals near embassies. When the French ambassador defied him in 1687, Innocent placed the ambassador under ecclesiastical censure. He also disapproved of the forcible methods used against Huguenots after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes.

sections.h2: The Relief of Vienna and the Holy League
paras: As the Ottoman army besieged Vienna in 1683, Innocent XI worked tirelessly to unite Emperor Leopold I and King John Sobieski of Poland and sent large subsidies. Their combined armies relieved Vienna on 12 September 1683. The pope then extended the feast of the Holy Name of Mary to the whole Church in thanksgiving.

In 1684 he formed the Holy League with the Empire, Poland and Venice, which went on to recover Buda in 1686. Innocent XI died on 12 August 1689. His cause for beatification was long delayed, partly by French opposition, and he was beatified by Pius XII on 7 October 1956. His feast is 12 August.

keyFacts: Born Benedetto Odescalchi in Como on 19 May 1611
Condemned 65 laxist moral propositions (1679)
Opposed the Gallican Articles of 1682
Helped unite the forces that relieved Vienna on 12 September 1683
Extended the feast of the Holy Name of Mary to the universal Church
Beatified by Pius XII on 7 October 1956

faqs.question: What role did Innocent XI play at the Battle of Vienna?
faqs.answer: He brokered the alliance between Emperor Leopold I and King John Sobieski and sent heavy subsidies. Their armies lifted the Ottoman siege on 12 September 1683.

faqs.question: Why was Innocent XI beatified?
faqs.answer: He was recognized for heroic virtue: personal austerity, charity to the poor, refusal of nepotism and zeal for reform. Pius XII beatified him in 1956.

faqs.question: What was mental reservation and why did Innocent XI condemn it?
faqs.answer: It was the practice of deceiving others by mentally adding unspoken qualifications to one's words, even under oath. Innocent XI condemned its abuse among 65 lax propositions in 1679.
